source_refs.note: Book p. 65: system (i), consistent and inconsistent systems, the three methods

blocks.text:
Three linear equations in three variables such as:
\[a_1x + b_1y + c_1z = d_1\]
\[a_2x + b_2y + c_2z = d_2\]
\[a_3x + b_3y + c_3z = d_3 \quad \text{...(i)}\]
is called a system of non-homogeneous linear equations in the three variables \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\), if constant terms \(d_1\), \(d_2\) and \(d_3\) are not all zero.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
"Non-homogeneous" only means that at least one right-hand side is not zero. If \(d_1 = d_2 = d_3 = 0\) the system is homogeneous; that case comes in Section 4.9.
In matrix language system (i) is \(AX = B\) with
\[A = \begin{bmatrix}a_1 & b_1 & c_1 \\ a_2 & b_2 & c_2 \\ a_3 & b_3 & c_3\end{bmatrix}\]
\[X = \begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix},\quad B = \begin{bmatrix}d_1 \\ d_2 \\ d_3\end{bmatrix}\]
\(A\) is the coefficient matrix. \(A\) with the column \(B\) attached is the augmented matrix. Non-homogeneous means \(B \ne O\).
Consistent: A system of linear equations is said to be consistent if the system has a unique solution or it has infinitely many solutions.
Inconsistent: A system of linear equations is said to be inconsistent if the system has no solution.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Three possibilities, seen with two variables (each equation is a straight line):
\(x + y = 2\), \(x - y = 0\): the lines cross at one point, \((1, 1)\). Unique solution, consistent.
\(x + y = 2\), \(2x + 2y = 4\): the second equation is the first one doubled, the lines coincide. Infinitely many solutions, consistent.
\(x + y = 2\), \(x + y = 3\): parallel lines, they never meet. No solution, inconsistent.
A linear system never has exactly two or three solutions: it is always one, infinitely many, or none.
Now we will solve the system of non-homogeneous linear equations with the help of the following methods:

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Which method when?
Reduced echelon form works for every system: unique, infinitely many or no solution. It also tells us which case we are in.
Matrix inversion and Cramer's rule need \(|A| \ne 0\); then the solution is unique. They are quick for \(3 \times 3\) systems with a non-zero determinant.
Each method has its own page: 4.8.1, 4.8.2 and 4.8.3.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Non-homogeneous system: \(AX = B\) with the constants \(d_1, d_2, d_3\) not all zero.
2. Consistent: a unique solution or infinitely many solutions.
3. Inconsistent: no solution.
4. Three methods: reduced echelon form, matrix inversion, Cramer's rule.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Thinking "consistent" means "unique solution". Infinitely many solutions is also consistent.
2. Calling a system homogeneous because one constant is zero. It is homogeneous only when all constants are zero.
3. Using matrix inversion or Cramer's rule when \(|A| = 0\). Then use the echelon method.
